title: Wake on change instead of polling an empty source
goal: Choose an event-driven trigger without confusing the wake-up signal with durable ingestion progress.
tag: Focused certification lesson · orchestration and ingestion · cycle 4, position 1
concept:
A shop can check the mailbox every minute, even when it is empty. Or the carrier can ring a bell when mail arrives.

Polling is the repeated mailbox check. An event-driven trigger is the bell. The bell starts work, but it does not remember which files or rows were safely processed. Durable ingestion state still belongs in Auto Loader checkpoints, a Snowflake Stream, or another explicit progress record.
example: Partner acme sends three order files at 09:00:00, 09:00:20, and 09:01:30. A 60-second quiet window groups the first two files into one run at 09:01:20. The third file starts another run at 09:02:30. The trigger decides when to wake; the ingestion state decides what remains.

use_case.when: Use change-driven orchestration when arrivals are irregular and frequent polling wastes compute or adds avoidable latency.
use_case.example: Wake a bronze-to-silver order pipeline when partner files or table changes appear instead of running an empty job every five minutes.
use_case.decision: Use a schedule when arrivals are predictable or the source cannot emit a trustworthy signal. Even with triggers, keep processing idempotent and store progress independently because notifications can be delayed, coalesced, or repeated.

practice: Change the arrival gap and quiet window. Predict whether three files create one run, two runs, or three runs before reading the timeline.
boundary: The local model groups three synthetic arrival times. It does not call cloud notifications, Lakeflow Jobs, Auto Loader, Snowflake Streams or Tasks; model delivery guarantees; calculate service cost; or prove exactly-once effects. Vendor configurations are sourced examples and were not executed.

Wake-up grouping only; processed-file state is separate.

';};arrivalGap.oninput=paintEvents;quietWindow.oninput=paintEvents;paintEvents();

Durable ingestion progress and idempotent writes

To guarantee every producer is finished forever
To replace schema validation
Debouncing trades a little latency for fewer partial-batch runs.

Arrivals are predictable or no dependable change signal exists
Every file has a unique name

A trigger adds machinery only when irregular arrivals justify it.

product_sections.title: Databricks: a file-arrival trigger wakes the job; Auto Loader remembers the files
product_sections.html:
Different jobs for different responsibilities. A Lakeflow Jobs file-arrival trigger monitors a Unity Catalog external location or volume. A quiet window can debounce a burst; a minimum interval caps run frequency. The triggered job can use Auto Loader with a checkpoint to discover and record files durably.

# sourced PySpark sketch; not executed here(spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles") .option("cloudFiles.format", "json") .load("/Volumes/ops/in/orders") .writeStream.option("checkpointLocation", checkpoint) .trigger(availableNow=True).toTable("ops.bronze.orders"))

Failure/fix. Overwriting an existing file with the same name does not trigger a file-arrival run. Prefer immutable file names and let Auto Loader track ingestion. High unrelated change volume above a monitored subpath can also hurt trigger evaluation; scope the external location or volume.

Execution label. PySpark is an unexecuted vendor sketch. The timeline is a local JavaScript teaching model.
product_sections.markdown: A file-arrival trigger decides when a Lakeflow Job starts. Auto Loader and its checkpoint decide which immutable files remain. Debounce with Wait after last change; cap frequency with Minimum time between triggers. The PySpark sketch was not run.

product_sections.title: Snowflake: a Stream exposes change; a triggered Task consumes it
product_sections.html:
The trigger watches a Stream, not a storage path. A triggered Task uses WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA(...) without a schedule. It starts suspended, so resume it. Snowflake runs one instance at a time and checks again after completion when more Stream data exists.

-- sourced SQL sketch; not executed hereCREATE TASK load_orders  TARGET_COMPLETION_INTERVAL = '15 MINUTES'  WHEN SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA('orders_delta')AS MERGE INTO silver.orders USING orders_delta ...;ALTER TASK load_orders RESUME;

Failure/fix. The task body must consume changes before the Stream becomes stale. A directory table also needs automatic or manual refresh before a triggered task can detect file changes. Monitor Stream age and task history; do not treat SYSTEM$STREAM_HAS_DATA as a row-count guarantee.

Execution label. No Snowflake SQL ran. The Stream/task diagram is a local teaching model.
product_sections.markdown: A triggered Task wakes when a Stream reports data. It has no schedule, starts suspended, and must be resumed. The task must consume changes before Stream retention expires. SQL was not executed.

title: Release the read lock before asking to write
goal: Avoid a read-to-write upgrade that cannot succeed; release, acquire the write lock, then recheck the condition.
concept:
You are reading a library book at a shared table. You cannot reserve the whole table while still claiming only a reader's seat, because other readers may be doing the same thing.

With Java's ReentrantReadWriteLock, a writer may acquire the read lock and downgrade safely. A reader cannot upgrade to the write lock. Release the read lock, acquire the write lock, and recheck because another writer may have changed the state in between.
example: Thread A reads configuration version 7 and decides it is stale. tryLock() on the write lock returns false while A holds the read lock. A releases read, takes write, then checks the version again before publishing version 8.

use_case.when: Use a read-write lock when reads are frequent, writes are shorter and less frequent, and measurement shows concurrent readers help.
use_case.example: Many request threads read a routing snapshot while one refresh thread occasionally replaces it.
use_case.decision: Prefer an immutable snapshot or simpler mutex unless profiling justifies the extra policy. Never design a read-to-write upgrade; release, acquire write, and revalidate.

practice: Toggle whether the reader releases before requesting write. Watch the lock state and the mandatory recheck.
boundary: The Java replay uses one thread and tryLock; it proves the documented upgrade result in this runtime, not fairness, contention throughput, starvation, scheduler order, memory costs, or application correctness.
js:
function paintLock(){const released=releaseRead.checked,v=+observedVersion.value;lockWorld.innerHTML='
A reads v7
'+(released?'release read':'still holds read')+'
write '+(released?'acquired':'cannot upgrade')+'
'+(released?'recheck: now v'+v:'no write, no publish')+'
';};releaseRead.onchange=paintLock;observedVersion.oninput=paintLock;paintLock();
questions: Thread A holds readLock and calls writeLock.tryLock(). Expected result?
It fails; read-to-write upgrade is unsupported
It always succeeds
It silently drops the read lock
A reader cannot upgrade to writer.
Why recheck after releasing read and acquiring write?
Another writer may have changed the protected state in the gap
The JVM forgets the key
Read locks do not see memory
The condition that justified writing may no longer hold.
When should you prefer a simple mutex?
Profiling does not show enough read concurrency to justify the policy complexity
There are multiple readers
The data is immutable
Read-write locks are a measured optimization, not a default.

steps.note: Create one read-write lock.
The current thread holds read; the write upgrade fails.
Release read, then acquire write.
Record the safe pattern and release write.

walkthrough.limit: The Java replay uses one thread and tryLock; it proves the documented upgrade result in this runtime, not fairness, contention throughput, starvation, scheduler order, memory costs, or application correctness.

visual_explanation: The lock-state sequence answers why an upgrade stalls and where another writer can intervene. The version slider makes the recheck necessary instead of ceremonial.
written_questions: Where does your code attempt a lock upgrade or perform I/O while holding a write lock?
Could an immutable snapshot remove the lock from the read path?

title: A risk acceptance needs an owner, a trigger, and an expiry
goal: Turn a permanent exception into a time-bounded decision that is re-evaluated when evidence or exposure changes.
concept:
A temporary road detour needs a sign saying who owns it and when it will be removed. Otherwise temporary becomes permanent.

Accepting risk is an informed response, not the absence of work. Record the residual risk, accountable approver, compensating controls, review date, and evidence that forces an earlier review. AWS Managed Services documents one-year validity for its risk acceptances; your policy can be shorter.
example: Platform waiver R-42 permits an unsigned internal image for 90 days while a legacy builder is replaced. The owner is the platform director. A public exposure, a critical CVE, or loss of runtime isolation reopens the decision immediately—even on day 20.

use_case.when: Use a formal acceptance when a known residual risk cannot be removed before a justified delivery deadline and an accountable authority can decide within stated tolerance.
use_case.example: A regulated data platform temporarily accepts a legacy deployment path while enforcing network isolation, image scanning and a dated migration plan.
use_case.decision: Mitigate or avoid when impact exceeds tolerance, controls are weak, ownership is unclear, or the exception has no credible retirement path. Acceptance is not a substitute for backlog neglect.

practice: Move the waiver age and toggle changed exposure. Watch the decision reopen from either time or evidence.
boundary: The model is a governance teaching aid, not a quantitative risk assessment, legal opinion, compliance authorization, threat model, or substitute for the organization's risk authority.
js:
function paintRisk(){const age=+riskAge.value,changed=exposureChanged.checked,reopen=age>=90||changed;riskWorld.innerHTML='
R-42 owner
platform director
age '+age+' / 90 days
evidence '+(changed?'changed':'unchanged')+'
'+(reopen?'reassess now':'acceptance still bounded')+'
';};riskAge.oninput=paintRisk;exposureChanged.onchange=paintRisk;paintRisk();

Reassess immediately because the evidence trigger changed
Wait until day 90
Delete the risk record
Expiry is the latest review, not protection from material change.
Why name an accountable approver?
Risk acceptance is a decision within authority, not an ownerless technical note
It guarantees no incident
It replaces compensating controls
Someone must own the residual-risk decision.
When is acceptance invalid as a strategy?
Impact exceeds tolerance and no credible controls or retirement path exist
A migration needs two sprints
The record has an ID
Acceptance cannot manufacture tolerability.

title: A child agent gets new input, not an isolated application state
goal: Keep structured delegation separate from state isolation when an agent is exposed as a tool.
tag: GenAI harness engineering · nested agent context
concept:
Giving a contractor a separate work order does not automatically give them a separate bank account.

In the OpenAI Agents SDK, a nested Agent.as_tool() run can receive distinct structured tool_input. But official context guidance says it does not receive an isolated copy of application state by default. Mutable local context can therefore be shared across parent, tools and nested runs.
example: The parent starts with budget 3. A research child receives only {topic: "orders"}, then decrements context.budget. The parent now sees 2. The structured input was narrow; the mutable application object was shared.

use_case.when: Use local context for dependencies and request-scoped policy that tools need but the model should not see.
use_case.example: Share a logger and usage budget across an orchestration run while passing a narrow research request to one child agent.
use_case.decision: Share state intentionally for accounting or coordination. Create a scoped copy, immutable view, or capability-limited facade when a child must not mutate parent-owned state. Do not call nested delegation a sandbox.

practice: Toggle shared versus copied context and let the child spend one unit. Watch which parent budget changes.
boundary: The browser models Python object aliasing. It does not run the Agents SDK, call a model or tool, provide OS/process isolation, serialize RunState, model approvals, or prove concurrency safety. The recorded Python example is local and synthetic.

parent input
full request
child tool_input
{topic: orders}
app state
'+(copied?'copied':'shared alias')+'
after spend
parent '+parent+' · child '+child+'
';};copyContext.onchange=paintContext;childSpend.oninput=paintContext;paintContext();

No; nested runs do not get an isolated copy by default

A new agent name

title: Horizontal liquid in, vertical vapor out: cool the hotspot without water
goal: Understand how a two-phase dielectric microfluidic manifold replenishes liquid and evacuates vapor near a chip hotspot.
concept:
A boiling pot cools only while fresh liquid reaches the hot surface and vapor can escape. If bubbles block the route, the surface dries out and temperature rises.

Researchers etched a horizontal-inlet, vertical-outlet microfluidic manifold into a chip substrate. Dielectric HFE-7100 flowed toward the hotspot, boiled, and vented upward. The paper reports critical heat flux up to 1,570 W/cm².
example: At a synthetic hotspot load of 1,200 W/cm², a 1,000 W/cm² comparison limit is exceeded by 200. The reported prototype limit leaves 370 W/cm² of experimental headroom. Headroom is not a deployment guarantee; it is only distance from the reported critical heat-flux point.

use_case.when: Use this research when evaluating embedded cooling for unusually high-power-density electronics where coolant electrical conductivity matters.
use_case.example: A laboratory accelerator chip has localized heat flux beyond conventional dielectric two-phase cooling capability.
use_case.decision: Treat the result as a research prototype. Production adoption needs pressure-drop, pump, seal, lifetime, contamination, manufacturability, serviceability and full-system energy evidence.

practice: Change hotspot load. Watch liquid replenishment, vertical vapor exit and remaining experimental headroom.
boundary: This original arithmetic model uses the paper's reported 1,570 W/cm² maximum and a round 1,000 W/cm² comparison. It does not reproduce geometry, flow rate, pressure, temperature, dryout physics, uncertainty, pumping power, fabrication yield, reliability, or a deployable cooling design.

'+margin+' W/cm²

title: Separate queue time from run time before buying faster runners
goal: Diagnose whether a slow GitHub Actions pipeline waits for capacity or spends time executing work.
concept:
A five-minute taxi ride can still take twenty minutes if the taxi arrives fifteen minutes late.

Pipeline duration has at least two parts: queue time before a job starts and run time after it starts. GitHub Actions performance metrics expose queue time, run time and failure rate. Fix the part that is actually slow.
example: Job integration-test is created at 10:00, starts at 10:07, and completes at 10:12. Total latency is 12 minutes: 7 queued and 5 running. A larger runner may shorten the five-minute work but cannot directly remove seven minutes of unavailable capacity.

use_case.when: Use queue/run/failure metrics when delivery latency grows, runner pools saturate, or teams argue about caching versus more capacity.
use_case.example: A self-hosted EKS runner group makes pull requests wait while test execution itself remains stable.
use_case.decision: Add or rebalance runner capacity for queue pressure; optimize code, cache or parallelism for run-time pressure; inspect flaky jobs when failure rate drives reruns. Use percentiles and slices, not only one average.

practice: Change queue and run minutes. Watch the dominant bottleneck and recommended first experiment.
boundary: The local model uses one job and simple thresholds. It does not query GitHub, calculate percentiles, account for approvals, concurrency groups, billing, retries, matrix fan-out, runner startup, cancellations, or critical-path dependencies.

queued '+q+'m

'+diagnosis+'

title: A streaming write may wait until the receiver reads
goal: Use gRPC flow control to bound in-flight streaming data without mistaking write acceptance for network delivery.
concept:
A warehouse stops loading boxes when the receiving dock is full. More boxes can move only after the receiver clears space.

gRPC flow control protects a streaming receiver from a faster sender. A write can wait, and handing a value to the framework does not prove that bytes already crossed the network. Unary RPCs do not use this streaming mechanism.
example: The receiver advertises room for two 1-unit messages. The sender offers m1, m2, and m3. The first two enter the window. m3 waits until the application reads one message and capacity is acknowledged.

use_case.when: Use streaming RPCs and their flow control when either side sends a sequence whose production rate can exceed consumption rate.
use_case.example: A metadata service streams table-lineage updates to a slower catalog indexer.
use_case.decision: Use unary RPC for one request/response. For streaming, keep reading while writing, bound application queues too, propagate deadlines/cancellation, and avoid manual flow control unless the language API and workload justify it.

practice: Change receiver capacity and message count. Watch which messages enter the window and which remain blocked.
boundary: This local credit model is not an HTTP/2 or gRPC implementation. It omits byte-sized windows, compression, batching, language-specific APIs, OS buffers, deadlines, cancellation, network failure, fairness and manual-flow-control races.
js:
function paintFlow(){const credits=+receiverCredits.value,count=+messageCount.value,sent=Math.min(credits,count),blocked=count-sent;flowWorld.innerHTML='
sender offers '+count+'
window admits '+sent+'
blocked '+blocked+'
receiver read → +1 credit
';};receiverCredits.oninput=paintFlow;messageCount.oninput=paintFlow;paintFlow();
questions: Receiver window holds two messages; sender offers three. What happens?
The third may wait until receiver capacity returns
All three are guaranteed on the wire
The RPC becomes unary
Flow control applies backpressure to the faster sender.
A write call returns. What is not proven?
That the message already crossed the network and was consumed
That the framework accepted the value
That the stream exists
Framework buffering and transport delivery are later stages.
How can manual synchronous flow control deadlock?
Both sides write heavily and neither reads to return capacity
Both sides use unique IDs
The receiver has a deadline
Progress requires reads as well as writes.

steps.note: The receiver has two units of capacity.
Two messages enter; m3 waits.
Reading m1 returns one unit of capacity.
m3 can now enter the window.

walkthrough.limit: This local credit model is not an HTTP/2 or gRPC implementation. It omits byte-sized windows, compression, batching, language-specific APIs, OS buffers, deadlines, cancellation, network failure, fairness and manual-flow-control races.

visual_explanation: The receiver window makes backpressure visible: offered messages split into admitted and blocked sets, and one receiver read releases one credit. It is a state transition, not a decorative request arrow.
written_questions: Which streaming handlers can produce faster than downstream consumers read?
Where are application-level queues bounded in addition to transport flow control?
